title: Tire warranty replacement threshold lower percentile
scenario_markdown: The tread lifespan of a heavy-duty commercial tire is normally distributed with mean $\mu = 60,000$ miles and standard deviation $\sigma = 8,000$ miles ($X \sim N(60000, 8000^2)$). The manufacturer wants to establish a mileage warranty limit $X_w$ such that only $2\%$ ($0.02$) of tires wear out before reaching the warranty threshold ($P(X \le X_w) = 0.02$). What warranty mileage should the company guarantee?
assumptions: Continuous normal distribution X ~ N(60000, 8000^2) in miles
Independent tire wear lifespans under normal driving conditions
Lower 2% tail corresponds to cumulative probability Phi(Z*) = 0.02

approval.notes: Reviewed lower tail quantile: Phi(-2.0537) = 0.02 (table Z = -2.05). Unstandardized warranty cutoff Xw = 60000 + (-2.0537)(8000) = 43,570 miles (or 43,600 with Z = -2.05). Analyzed business cost implication of shifting threshold to 50k miles (claim rate jumps to 10.56%).
approval.delegation_basis: Content backlog Batch 1: Row 3.2 normal distribution expansion

stages.prompt_markdown: What standard score $Z^*$ corresponds to the lower $2\%$ tail of the normal distribution ($P(Z \le Z^*) = 0.02$)?

options.hint_markdown: A positive $Z$-score corresponds to a value above the mean ($98\text{th}$ percentile), not the bottom $2\%$.
$-2.326$ corresponds to a $1\%$ lower tail, not $2\%$.
$-0.02$ confuses the probability area ($0.02$) with the standardized coordinate on the horizontal axis.

stages.explanation_markdown: By symmetry and cumulative normal tables, the standard score with $2\%$ cumulative probability in the lower tail satisfies $\Phi(Z^*) = 0.02$. Looking up $0.02$ in the standard normal table gives $Z^* \approx -2.05$ (software gives $-2.05375$). Excel formula: `=NORM.S.INV(0.02)`.

stages.prompt_markdown: Using $Z^* \approx -2.054$, what is the warranty mileage cutoff $X_w = \mu + Z^* \sigma$?

options.hint_markdown: A warranty protects early failures, so the threshold must lie below the average lifespan.
Subtracting exactly one standard deviation leaves $15.87\%$ of tires below the threshold, far exceeding the $2\%$ target.
Percentiles of a normal distribution are non-linear and depend on standard deviations, not a direct percentage reduction of the mean.

stages.explanation_markdown: $X_w = \mu + Z^* \sigma = 60000 + (-2.05375)(8000) = 60000 - 16430 = 43,570\text{ miles}$ (or $43,600\text{ miles}$ with 2-decimal table rounding $Z = -2.05$). Excel formula: `=NORM.INV(0.02, 60000, 8000)` yields $43,570.01\text{ miles}$.

stages.prompt_markdown: If the company instead set an overly aggressive warranty limit at $50,000\text{ miles}$, how would this affect warranty claim replacement rates?

options.text_markdown: Warranty claims would increase sharply from $2\%$ to approximately $10.56\%$, because $Z = \frac{50000 - 60000}{8000} = -1.25$ and $\Phi(-1.25) \approx 0.1056$.
Warranty claims would decrease because $50,000\text{ miles}$ is below the average tire lifespan of $60,000\text{ miles}$.
options.hint_markdown: Raising the warranty mileage increases the proportion of tires that fail before reaching the limit.

options.text_markdown: Warranty claims would remain at exactly $2\%$ because the manufacturer can contractually limit replacements.
options.hint_markdown: The failure rate is determined by the physical distribution of tire wear relative to the declared warranty threshold.

stages.explanation_markdown: At $X = 50000\text{ miles}$, $Z = \frac{50000 - 60000}{8000} = -1.25$. From normal distribution tables, $P(X \le 50000) = \Phi(-1.25) \approx 0.10565$ (or $10.56\%$). Raising the warranty limit by only $6,430$ miles increases warranty replacements more than five-fold, highlighting the steep curvature of the normal distribution tail.
